newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU states may bar goods with misleading trade marks - court.
newsitem.headline: EU states may bar goods with misleading trade marks - court.

text.p: European Union governments may under certain circumstances bar products from other EU states if they carry trademarks that have been banned for misleading consumers, the the European Court of Justice said on Tuesday.
The court was ruling in a case involving toilet paper and disposable handerchiefs produced by Scott Paper Co that had been marketed in Italy under the trade mark "Cotonelle".
An Italian court ordered Scott to stop using the name on the grounds that it might mislead consumers into thinking the products actually contained cotton.

However, Ditta Fransa, which owns a supermarket in the province of Genoa, continued marketing Cotonelle products imported from France. Fratelli Graffione SNC, a wholesaler that had stopped selling Cotonelle, filed suit to stop Fransa on the grounds of unfair competition.
An Italian court asked the Court of Justice to rule on whether the products could be kept out under EU law.

The court said that Articles 30 and 36 of the EC treaty on the free movement of goods allowed governments to bar products that are legally marketed in other EU states on grounds of consumer protection, as long as the move was proportionate and the objective could not be achieved by less restrictive measures.

It said Council Directive 89/104/EEC (the Trade Mark Directive) allowed governments to bar goods on the grounds that they bear a trade mark that has been banned in the importing state for misleading consumers.
EXCERPTS FROM THE JUDGMENT

"Prohibition of the use of a trade mark in a Member State - Prohibition of importation from another Member State of a product bearing the same trade mark - Article 30 of the EC Treaty and the Trade Mark Directive"
In Case C-313/94
Reference to the Court under Article 177 of the EC Treaty by the Tribunale di Chiavari, Italy, for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings pending before that court between
Fratelli Graffione SNC
and
Ditta Fransa

on the interpretation of Articles 30 and 36 of the EC Treaty and Article 12(2)(b) of the First Council Directive 89/104/EEC of 21 December 1988 to approximate the laws of the Member States relating to trade marks (OJ 1989 L 40, p. 1)
THE COURT hereby rules
1. Articles 30 and 36 of the EC Treaty are to be interpreted as

- precluding reliance on protection against unfair competition as a ground for prohibiting an undertaking from using its right to import into a Member State products coming from another Member State where they are lawfully marketed and to market them under a particular trade mark in the Member State of importation, when other traders have the same right, even if they do not use it;

- but not precluding a prohibition, on grounds of consumer protection, on the marketing by all traders of products coming from a Member State where they are lawfully marketed, provided that the prohibition is necessary in order to ensure consumer protection and proportionate to that objective, which must be incapable of being achieved by measures which are less restrictive of intra-Community trade. The national court must, in particular, examine whether the risk of misleading consumers is sufficiently serious to be able to override the requirements of the free movement of goods.

2. Article 12(2)(b) of Council Directive 89/104/EEC of 21 December 1998 to approximate the laws of the Member States relating to trade marks is to be interpreted as not precluding a prohibition on the marketing of products coming from a Member State where they are lawfully marketed, on the ground that they bear a trade mark which the proprietor has been specfically prohibited from using in the Member State of importation because it has been held there to be liable to mislead consumers.
